strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive and mathematically rigorous classification of parameterized complexity across the 3x3 expressivity matrix of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH).

The algorithmic approach for SAT_prob^lin departs from standard leaf-to-root dynamic programming over tree decompositions, instead synthesizing a structural causal model via an elegant, treewidth-guided linear program.

The upper bounds are matched with tight parameterized and classical hardness results (e.g., establishing that moving from probabilistic to causal reasoning causes hardness even on graphs of pathwidth 1 with binary domains, ruling out treewidth-based tractability for SAT_causal^lin).
The paper is exceptionally well-written and well-organized, with clear exposition and a very helpful running example (Example 6) that grounds the linear programming construction.
weaknesses: The work is purely theoretical; there is no empirical evaluation or implementation demonstrating the practical feasibility of the LP constructions on actual causal reasoning benchmarks.

For the counterfactual fragment, tractability requires parameterization by the total number of endogenous variables n, and the resulting algorithm incurs an n! · d^{O(n^2)} runtime overhead, which significantly restricts applicability to small models.
The manuscript appears to be prepared using the LIPIcs template rather than the standard ICML style guidelines.

strengths: The paper initiates the parameterized complexity analysis of satisfiability across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH), filling an important gap between known classical intractability results (NP-completeness and ETR-completeness) and practical tractability.

The theoretical results provide a comprehensive classification of tractability and hardness across both dimensions of the PCH (depth: probabilistic, causal, counterfactual; breadth: base, linear, polynomial) under natural structural parameters (primal treewidth, domain size, and number of variables).

The algorithmic approach for Theorem 5 departs innovatively from traditional leaf-to-root dynamic programming over tree decompositions, instead constructing a compact linear program whose solution provably guarantees the existence of a valid Structural Causal Model (SCM).
The manuscript is clearly written and logically structured, featuring a clear summary mind map (Figure 1), concrete illustrative examples (Example 6), and complete mathematical proofs.
weaknesses: The positive treewidth-based tractability results are confined strictly to the observational probabilistic fragment (SAT_prob^lin); as shown in Theorem 9, the causal and counterfactual layers remain NP-hard even on disjoint paths of length 2, requiring the significantly stronger parameterization by the total number of variables n.

The paper is entirely theoretical, lacking an empirical evaluation or implementation demonstrating the practical scalability of the LP formulations on real-world or synthetic causal reasoning benchmarks.

strengths: Provides the first comprehensive parameterized complexity map for satisfiability across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH), delineating exact boundaries between fixed-parameter tractability (FPT), slice-wise polynomial tractability (XP), and intractability.

Technically rigorous and creative approach: departing from the conventional dynamic programming paradigm on tree decompositions, the authors develop a treewidth-guided linear programming approach for probabilistic satisfiability, showing that local consistency on nice tree decompositions provably admits a valid structural causal model.

Tight lower bounds accompany the positive results, featuring elegant reductions—such as using causal intervention constraints on disjoint paths of length 2 to force topological ordering for 3-SAT (Theorem 9), and proving existential theory of the reals (∃R) hardness even when the primal graph is completely edgeless (Theorem 2).
Paper is exceptionally well-written, clearly organized, and contextualizes its contributions thoroughly with respect to prior work on causal satisfiability and parameterized algorithms.
weaknesses: Purely theoretical contribution without empirical evaluation or benchmark implementation demonstrating the practical scalability of the LP formulations on real-world causal formulas.
The parameter dependence in the positive algorithms involves significant overhead (e.g., d^{O(n^2)} or d^{O(tw)}), which limits immediate applicability to very small parameter regimes.
The manuscript is prepared using the LIPIcs LaTeX template rather than standard conference format and significantly exceeds standard conference page limits.

strengths: The paper provides the first comprehensive parameterized complexity classification for the satisfiability problem across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH), establishing an elegant and complete map of tractability and intractability borders.

The algorithmic technique in Theorem 5 is novel and elegant: rather than following standard leaf-to-root dynamic programming on tree decompositions, it constructs a compact linear program over bag-consistent marginal distributions and reconstructs the underlying SCM constructively via BFS.

The paper provides matching parameterized hardness results (e.g., W[1]-hardness with respect to variable count, NP-hardness with bounded degree, and ∃R-hardness for polynomial fragments even with n=1), demonstrating that the positive FPT and XP results are essentially tight.
The manuscript is clearly written and very well structured, with an informative roadmap (Figure 1) and a pedagogical walkthrough of the LP construction (Example 6).
weaknesses: The algorithm for counterfactual satisfiability (SATlin counterfact, Theorem 11) incurs a doubly-exponential parameter dependence on n (O(d^{d^n}) LP variables), which limits its practical applicability to very small values of n.
The work is purely theoretical with no implementation or experimental evaluation demonstrating the feasibility of the LP formulations on benchmark or synthetic causal formulas.

There are minor citation/labeling inconsistencies in the text: for example, on page 16, the proof of Theorem 11 refers to 'Theorem 3' (which is Observation 3) and repeatedly refers to 'Theorem 10' (which is labeled Lemma 10).

strengths: Presents the first systematic parameterized complexity analysis of the satisfiability problem across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH), filling a significant gap between known intractability results and practical tractability.

Provides a comprehensive and elegant landscape (summarized clearly in Figure 1) with matching upper bounds (FPT/XP algorithms) and conditional lower bounds (NP-completeness, W[1]-hardness, and Existential Theory of the Reals completeness) across the expressivity matrix.

Technically innovative: deviates from standard dynamic programming on tree decompositions by formulating a tree-decomposition-guided Linear Program with consistency constraints and proving that every valid LP solution can be mapped back to an explicit Structural Causal Model (SCM).
Clear, rigorous, and well-structured exposition, supported by concrete and instructive examples (e.g., Example 6 explaining the LP construction and SCM recovery).
weaknesses: The work is purely theoretical with no implementation or experimental evaluation to benchmark the practical performance and scalability of the proposed LP formulations.

The FPT algorithm for counterfactual satisfiability (SAT_counterfact^lin) has a double-exponential parameter dependence (running time n!(|phi|^O(1) + d^O(d^n))), which is practically prohibitive for anything beyond very small n and d.

The positive tractability results rely strictly on formulas being conjunctions (sets) of inequalities, as arbitrary Boolean combinations (arbSAT) remain intractable even in trivial topologies, which limits the logical expressiveness in some potential applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental open question in the theory of causal inference: establishing the boundaries of tractability for the satisfiability of formulas across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (PCH) through the lens of parameterized complexity.

The theoretical results provide a comprehensive and tight mapping of parameterized complexity across both dimensions of the PCH expressivity matrix (depth: probabilistic, causal, counterfactual; breadth: base, linear, polynomial).

The algorithmic techniques depart notably from standard dynamic programming over tree decompositions by constructing a compact linear program over bag configurations and synthesizing consistent exogenous variables, which elegantly integrates discrete graph structure with continuous probability distributions.

The paper is very well structured and mathematically rigorous, providing self-contained proofs and clear matching hardness results (including ∃R-completeness for polynomial fragments and W[1]-hardness for variable count).
weaknesses: The primary positive result utilizing graph structure (treewidth) only applies to the probabilistic fragment (SAT_prob^lin). For the causal and counterfactual fragments—which are the core objects of interest in causal inference—Theorem 9 proves that bounding treewidth does not avoid NP-hardness even for matching/disjoint graphs of treewidth 1.

The FPT algorithm for the counterfactual fragment (Theorem 11) exhibits an upper bound of O(n! * (poly + d^{O(d^n)})), which is doubly exponential in the number of variables n. This makes the tractability purely classification-theoretic rather than practically usable, even for very small models (e.g., n = 4 or 5).

The paper is prepared in LIPIcs format (running to 19 pages) rather than the standard ICML conference format, and reads more like a pure theoretical computer science / parameterized algorithms contribution than a machine learning paper, lacking experimental implementation or discussion of practical causal modeling workflows.
